title: The mental state examination
blurb: Carry out and record a structured mental state examination, using the right term for what you see and hear.
question: Mr Danso, 38, sits slumped and tearful and speaks slowly, but tells the nurse, 'I'm fine, honestly.' He says his food is being poisoned by his neighbours and he is certain of it. How should the nurse record these findings in the mental state examination?

teach.body: The mental state examination (MSE) is a structured description of a person's mental state at the time of assessment, based on what you observe and what they tell you. It is to mental health what a set of vital signs is to physical health: a snapshot, recorded under standard headings, that can be compared over time. In plain English: you describe exactly what you see and hear, in the person's words where possible, without jumping to a diagnosis.
teach.cite: Standard RCPsych MSE teaching; NMC MSE OSCE station

teach.caption: When the two do not match (says 'fine', looks very low), record the affect as incongruent with the reported mood.

head: Term
What you notice
rows: Rapid jumps linked by rhymes, puns or sounds (often mania)
Ideas with no logical link between them
Fast, hard to interrupt (recorded under speech)
Very few ideas, short empty answers

teach.h: Thought content: what thoughts are about
head: Term
Key feature
rows: Fixed false belief, held despite evidence, out of keeping with culture
Strongly held, understandable belief that dominates life
Intrusive thought the person sees as their own and resists
Always asked about and recorded, with plans

rows.label: Example
values: Coat on a door seen as a man

teach.caption: A pseudohallucination is experienced as coming from inside the mind ('in my head') rather than from outside.

teach.body: Nurse Okeke writes: Appearance: unkempt, slumped, poor eye contact. Speech: slow, quiet, reduced quantity. Mood: 'I'm fine, honestly.' Affect: low, tearful, incongruent with stated mood. Thought content: fixed belief that neighbours are poisoning his food (delusion); asked about suicidal thoughts. Perception: denies hearing voices. Cognition: orientated. Insight: does not see himself as unwell. She records exact quotes and escalates the risk of food refusal.

teach.text: Two classic mix-ups. Mood is what the PERSON says; affect is what YOU observe. And thought FORM is how thoughts are linked (flight of ideas, thought block), while thought CONTENT is what the thoughts are about (delusions, obsessions). A delusion is content, even when it is about thoughts being taken away.

items: Do you think anything has changed in you recently?
Do you think this could be an illness?
Do you think treatment or hospital could help?
Record full, partial or no insight, with the person's own words.
Headings: appearance and behaviour, speech, mood and affect, thought form and content, perception, cognition, insight.
Mood is reported; affect is observed; note any incongruence.
Form = how thoughts connect; content = what they are about.
Hallucination has no stimulus; an illusion misperceives a real one.
Use the person's exact words and always record risk alongside.

summary: You can now carry out a structured mental state examination and record findings under the correct headings. You can distinguish mood from affect, thought form from content, and hallucinations from illusions, and record insight and risk.

A.q: In the mental state examination, what does 'affect' describe?
options: The person's own account of how they feel
The emotional state the clinician observes
How logically the person's thoughts connect
The person's understanding of their illness
A.why: Affect is the clinician's objective observation of emotional expression (range, reactivity, congruence); mood is the person's own description.

whyNot.0: That is mood, the subjective report.

A.q: A patient says, 'The TV presenter sends me messages through the screen,' and cannot be persuaded otherwise. Under which MSE heading is this recorded?
A.why: A fixed false belief held despite evidence is a delusion, recorded under thought content (here a delusion of reference).

whyNot.0: Perception covers sensory experiences such as hallucinations, not beliefs.
whyNot.1: Thought form describes how thoughts link, not what they are about.
whyNot.3: Cognition covers orientation, attention and memory.

A.q: On a dark ward at night, Mrs Bell sees a dressing gown on the door and is sure it is a man. When the light is on she sees it is a gown. What is this?
A.why: An illusion is a misperception of a real external stimulus, common in poor light, fear or delirium.

whyNot.0: A pseudohallucination is experienced as arising inside the mind.
whyNot.1: A hallucination occurs without any real stimulus; here the gown is real.
whyNot.2: She corrects the belief when the light is on, so it is not a fixed belief.

B.q: Ms Lee, 27, speaks very quickly: 'I took the train, train of thought, thought police, police dogs bark at the dark park.' Which term best describes her thought form?
B.why: Flight of ideas: rapid shifts between ideas linked by rhymes, puns or word associations, typical of mania.

whyNot.0: Thought block is a sudden stop in the flow of thought.
whyNot.1: In loosening of associations there is no recognisable link; here the links are sound and word associations.
whyNot.2: Poverty of thought is a lack of ideas, the opposite of this.

B.q: Mr Ali, 23, stops speaking abruptly mid-sentence several times, then starts a new topic. How should this be recorded?
B.why: A sudden interruption in the flow of thought with speech stopping mid-sentence is thought block, recorded under thought form.

whyNot.1: Poverty of speech is a reduced quantity of speech overall, not abrupt stops.
whyNot.2: Thought insertion is a belief (content), not a perceptual experience, and is not described here.
whyNot.3: Cognitive inattention would not explain an abrupt stop and new topic.

B.q: Ms Wu, detained under section 3, says: 'The voices are an illness and the tablets help, but I don't need to be in hospital.' How is her insight best recorded?
B.why: She accepts that she is ill and that treatment helps but not the need for admission: partial insight.

whyNot.0: Full insight would include accepting the need for the current care setting.
whyNot.1: She does recognise illness and the benefit of medication.
whyNot.3: Her statement is about insight, not orientation, attention or memory.

C.q: Mr Hughes, 52, tells the nurse during his MSE that a man's voice outside his head is telling him to hurt his wife. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Record it as a pseudohallucination and continue
Ask about the commands and whether he can resist
Reassure him that the voice is not real
Complete the cognition section before risk
C.why: Command hallucinations to harm others are a key risk finding. The nurse explores content, frequency and his ability to resist, records his words, and escalates to the team.

whyNot.0: A voice heard outside the head is a true hallucination, and the risk needs exploring, not just recording.
whyNot.2: Arguing that the voice is not real does not assess or manage the risk.
whyNot.3: Risk to his wife takes priority over finishing other headings.

C.q: Mrs Grant, 81, admitted with low mood, cannot say the day or month, keeps losing track of questions and was well yesterday. Under which heading do these findings belong, and what do they suggest?
C.why: Disorientation and inattention are recorded under cognition; acute onset with inattention points to possible delirium, which needs a 4AT and a search for a physical cause (NICE CG103).

whyNot.0: Disorientation is a cognitive finding, not a disorder of thought form.
whyNot.2: Low mood alone does not explain sudden disorientation and inattention.
whyNot.3: Insight concerns understanding of illness, not orientation.

C.q: A student writes: 'Mood: low. Affect: low.' The patient actually said, 'I feel absolutely fine,' while appearing tearful and flat. What is the best correction?
options: Mood: low, as observation overrides his words
Affect: fine, matching his own description
Mood and affect: both normal on his account
C.why: Mood records the person's own words; affect records the observed state. When they do not match, note the incongruence.

whyNot.1: Mood is the person's report; the observation belongs under affect.
whyNot.2: Affect is what the clinician observes, which was tearful and flat.
whyNot.3: His account cannot override what was observed for affect.

reteach.title: Say what you see, quote what you hear
reteach.question: How do you keep MSE terms straight?

blocks.body: Ask: did the person tell me this, or did I observe it? Their words go in mood and content, quoted; your observations go in appearance, affect and speech. Then ask: is this about HOW thoughts link (form) or WHAT they are about (content)? Finally, is there a real stimulus (illusion) or none (hallucination)?

blocks.text: A delusion is recorded under thought content, not perception.

explain.body: Describe self-care, clothing, eye contact, movement and rapport. For speech, note rate, volume, tone and quantity. Pressured speech is fast and hard to interrupt.

test.q: A patient speaks rapidly and loudly, and the nurse struggles to get a word in. How is this recorded?
test.why: Rapid, loud speech that is hard to interrupt is pressure of speech, recorded under speech.

whyNot.1: Flight of ideas is thought form and is not a perceptual finding.
whyNot.2: Affect is not part of cognition, and this describes speech.
whyNot.3: Thought block is a sudden stop and belongs under form.

explain.body: Mood is the person's own description of how they have been feeling. Affect is the emotional expression you observe, including range, reactivity and whether it fits the stated mood (congruence).

options: Mood: flat with poor eye contact
test.why: Mood is recorded in the person's own words; the other entries describe observations.

whyNot.0: Tearful and restricted are observations of affect.
whyNot.2: Congruence is described when recording affect against mood.
whyNot.3: Flatness and eye contact are observed, so they belong under affect and appearance.

explain.body: Form describes how thoughts are linked: flight of ideas, loosening of associations, thought block. Content describes what the thoughts are about: delusions, overvalued ideas, obsessions, suicidal or homicidal thoughts.

test.q: Which finding belongs under thought content?
test.why: Obsessions are intrusive thoughts the person recognises as their own; they describe what is thought about, so they are content.

whyNot.0: Loosening of associations is a disorder of form.
whyNot.1: Thought block is a disorder of form.
whyNot.3: Flight of ideas is a disorder of form.

explain.body: Perception: hallucinations (no stimulus), illusions (misperceived real stimulus), pseudohallucinations (experienced inside the mind). Cognition: orientation, attention, memory. Insight: whether the person sees themselves as unwell and needing help.

test.q: A patient hears his name called in an empty, silent room. Which term applies?
test.why: Hearing a voice with no external stimulus is an auditory hallucination, recorded under perception.

whyNot.0: An illusion needs a real stimulus that is misperceived.
whyNot.1: A delusion of reference is a belief, recorded under content.
whyNot.2: An overvalued idea is a strongly held belief, not a perception.
